own_scenes.desc: En 1985 la energía se ha disipado: el new pop cae en la decadencia (Live Aid, «una tragedia para el pop»), los singles independientes venden la mitad que en 1980 y «independiente» se convierte en «indie», un género de guitarras sucias, voces pálidas y nostalgia de los sesenta, oposición impotente al mainstream. El futurismo da paso al «rock de coleccionista»: The Jesus and Mary Chain (Psychocandy: Ronettes y Beach Boys con feedback), el sello Creation y Primal Scream, la cassette C86 de NME (The Pastels, Shop Assistants, The Soup Dragons, June Brides) y su culto a la inocencia, que reaparecerá en el riot grrrl. The Smiths y R.E.M., contra los ochenta; Hüsker Dü, Sonic Youth, Butthole Surfers y Dinosaur Jr. redescubren el acid rock; de ahí, Nirvana.

refs.q: Lo más deprimente de 1985, sin embargo, no fue la decadencia del pop
refs.para: Lo más deprimente de 1985, sin embargo, no fue la decadencia del pop mainstream, sino la del underground. Ya no quedaban rastros del fervor y la convicción colectiva que habían unificado las diversas iniciativas postpunk.

refs.q: El desplazamiento semántico de lo "independiente" a lo "indie" merece un párrafo aparte
refs.para: El desplazamiento semántico de lo "independiente" a lo "indie" merece un párrafo aparte. "Independiente" alguna vez fue un término neutro que hacía referencia a las condiciones de producción y distribución de los discos. En 1 985, "indie" ya era un género musical, o un conjunto de subgéneros, con parámetros cada vez más reducidos. El rótulo "college rock" [rock universitario]

refs.q: Los miembros de The Jesus and Mary Chain fueron pioneros en este nuevo género
refs.para: Los miembros de The Jesus and Mary Chain fueron pioneros en este nuevo género, ya que básicamente sampleaban sin siquiera tener un sampler.

refs.q: Primal Scream era un ícono de la escena que muchos bautizaron "cutie"
refs.para: Primal Scream era un ícono de la escena que muchos bautizaron "cutie", "shambling" o, simplemente, CB6. Este último nombre provenía del cassette editado por NME -una alusión a su seminal recopilación anterior, CBJ-que documentaba el resurgimiento de bandas de noise pop indie que estalló a comienzos de 1 985 y culminó el año siguiente. Si bien The Jesus and Mary Chain habían sido los pioneros de esta corriente, y la década del sesenta su mayor punto de referencia, los grupos de C86 -The Soup Dragons, The Pastels, June Brides, Shop Assistants- también habían recibido el influjo de bandas postpunk como Swell Maps, Buzzcocks, Subway Sect, The Fall y muchas de las editadas por el sello Postcard. Sin embargo, se trataba de una versión del postpunk pur- gada de sus aspectos más radicales: la política, la fusión interracial y la experimentación en el estudio. Por ejemplo, dejaban de lado la combinación de disco y funk de Orange Juice, pero adoptaban el sonido de sus guitarras y la candidez ascética de Edwyn Collins.

podcast.title: Disagreement on the Term
podcast.body: Despite its usage, the phrase "College Rock" was not universally accepted, indicating a search for a more definitive and encompassing term for this new wave of music. "But not everyone could agree on that phrase."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early R.E.M. Style (1980s)
podcast.body: R.E.M. began their career as a college rock band, also characterized as indie alternative. This designation highlights their early roots in the independent music scene before their transition to a major label. "They started as an indie alternative band, a college rock band."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 2: (90-81)

podcast.title: Evolution to Indie/Alternative
podcast.body: As the 1980s progressed, the term "college rock" became outdated. The artists previously labeled as such began to be referred to as "indie groups," and their distinct sound and independent label affiliations led to their categorization as an "alternative" to mainstream offerings, thus giving rise to the term "alternative music." "Eventually, the term college rock didn't really cut it anymore. People began referring to these artists as indie groups."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Post-Punk Explosion Part 7: All the rest

podcast.title: Growth and Transition to Major Labels
podcast.body: College rock was a significant scene where bands like R.E.M. were pioneers, achieving respect and accessibility. R.E.M.'s eventual move to Warner Brothers, a major label, demonstrated that a college rock band could maintain integrity while gaining wider distribution. Sonic Youth, another cool group in the indie crowd, also made a successful leap to DGC, a Geffen subsidiary, influencing other indie bands, including Nirvana, to follow suit and change the course of music in the 1990s. "R.E.M. became the biggest of the so-called college rock indie bands to make the jump to a multi-million dollar major record label."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 8

podcast.title: Interchangeability with Alternative Rock (Mid-1980s)
podcast.body: For a period in the mid-1980s, "college rock" was used interchangeably with "alternative rock," driven by the growing influence of campus radio stations in promoting new music. This era saw independent labels embracing a loose, raw, and unpolished recording approach, often seen as cheap and primitive but considered cool for its unfancy and reactionary nature. "This was the era of college rock, which for a while was an interchangeable term with alternative rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Late 70s/Early 80s Phenomenon
podcast.body: College Rock was a distinct music category in the late 1970s and early 1980s, primarily played on campus radio stations across the US and Canada. It featured unsigned acts or those on independent labels, characterized by an "underground vibe," experimentalism, and a departure from mainstream radio sounds. "This was the material played on campus radio stations throughout the US and Canada in the late 70s and early 80s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Post-Punk Explosion Part 7: All the rest

podcast.title: Limiting Terminology
podcast.body: The term "college rock" eventually proved to be somewhat limiting, particularly for listeners who were not attending college. This limitation contributed to the subsequent adoption of broader and more inclusive terms like "alternative" and "Indy" for non-mainstream rock music. "But that seemed a little limiting, especially for people who weren't in college."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Predecessor to "Alternative" and "Indy"
podcast.body: For a period throughout the 1980s and 1990s, non-mainstream rock was sometimes called "college rock." This term was used because it represented the kind of music predominantly heard on campus radio stations, with bands like R.E.M. and The Pixies beginning their careers in this scene. "For a while, some called it college rock because it seemed to be the kind of music that you heard on campus radio stations."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Term Coined for College Radio Staples
podcast.body: The term "College Rock" emerged to describe music by bands like R.E.M., The Replacements, Husker Dü, and Sonic Youth, which were regularly featured on campus radio stations. This phrase reflected the music's popularity within the college radio network. "Since REM and the replacements in Husker Dew and Sonic Youth and their ilk were staples of college radio stations, this music began to be called College Rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Term Supplanted by Alternative
podcast.body: "College rock" was a term used to describe music favored by campus radio stations, but it was eventually supplanted by the term "alternative." "This word alternative eventually supplanted the term college rock, which was being used to describe the music that found favor with campus radio stations."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: University Radio Origins
podcast.body: In the 1980s, College Rock was primarily played on "America's student-run university campus radio stations," with bands like R.E.M. serving as key figures and "college town rock gods." "what was commonly known in the 80s as College Rock, typically played on America's student-run university campus radio stations."
